As someone who used to work at a store that carried most of the brands mentioned here, I have to say that while heavyweight tees are attractive, they're not always practical, especially in warm weather. A thicker cotton shirt doesn't automatically mean it will last longer, since durability mostly depends on the fabric's tensile strength and how well the ribbing is reinforced.
In my experience, light to mid-weight tees strike the best balance. Right off the bat, l'd say Warehouse offers the best value, though the neck can feel a bit tight for some. The Real McCoy's Loopwheel American Athletic tees have the best hand feel but can be a bit “nippy” for some. Samurai's organic cotton tees are my favorite in terms of feel, weight, and fit, though they do run slightly slim if you prefer a boxier silhouette.
They actually grow their own cotton and use vegetable dyes, and since they're sold in 2-piece packs, they're honestly some of the best you can buy for the money.

Torque is natural to any circular knit fabric. Getting rid of it usually requires a fabric rinse at the mill, then at least a 48 hour relaxing period at the factory when the fabric is received, prior to cutting the panels.  Cutting these steps out saves money and time for a brand and the customer won’t find out until after a home laundry cycle.

One thing worth noting with Asian/Japanese brands is that they're often designed for a smaller frame. I have what can be diplomatically be called a "Western Build" (I'm tall, broad shoulders, barrel chested, etc) and I found shirts in particular were extremely awkward to buy in Asia (I lived there for several years). A "large" size shirt would have narrow shoulders. An XL shirt would have a baggy chest. It's something to bear in mind when buying; especially if you're importing a $200 shirt, because those returns can get expensive. If you're a big dude, the fit can be weird.
